title: Eureka with Bhaskar from Rammur
description: In conversation with Dr. Bhaskar Ramamurthi, Director, IIT-Madras.   Dr. Ramamurthi is an academician who has been the Director of Indian Institute of Technology-Madras from 2011. His area of expertise lies in Electronics Engineering and has contributed significantly in the WLL project.   Anchor: Gauhar Raza

asr.full_text: Hello and welcome I am Gauhar Raza and you are watching Eureka. When you think of wireless you. Think of JC Bose in India. First rate scientist which India produced long ago and before Marconi. He could demonstrate that things can be done remotely. His experiment was published but he. Did not demonstrate it as a science experiment. He wanted to impress upon the British Raj that. Firstly science can be done in India, technology can be developed in India itself. However, a lot. Of water has flown down the Ganges. We have first-rate scientists and technologists who. Are working in the area. Welcome Dr. Bhaskar. I'm extremely thankful that you. Gave time to us. Your journey to become a communication engineer, electronics. Engineer and then director of the Institute where you studied initially. Has been ridden with a lot of twists and turns. You wanted to become a pilot. And then you became an engineer. Was it a trauma when your mother said,. No, you are not going to be a pilot? No, I shouldn't say it was a trauma. Because I wasn't very clear about what I wanted to be. And it turned out that there were a couple of cousins. Who had joined the Air Force. And they used to come by every now and then. And that seemed attractive to me. I had joined the NCC in school. But I think not only my mother,. Some of my friends also told me that you are doing well in studies and you should do something else. And I was an amenable kid and I think once they all told me, I said, okay, that's fine. I was also. Apprehensive because I was very puny. I was barely five feet, three and a half inches when I came. I was just a good student, that's all, you know. I think it was just a question, you know, one of. The top students in class so I was just and you know it was very clear to me that's you. Know I was I was sort of interested in physics chemistry and so on and not that much interested. In accounts and so on so that was very clear and my dad never you know never really asked. Was it because of the teachers? Possibly you know I think. You don't remember some teachers. Well I do remember them I think they were very good and I'm not saying I mean I really. Don't know see in those days it was not there was this 10 plus 2 system was not there so. You didn't have to choose commerce in school so I think I could have gone you know it's. I don't think there was any difference between, yeah there was a commerce section and there. Was a science section and all the good students always went to the science section. Yes, but the students never went to commerce. So that's how I migrated there. I don't think there was any well thought out process and then they told me to write IIT. So I started looking at the syllabus and so on, it looked interesting. So fortunately in those days this ISC used to be, the exams used to finish in December. So we had a five month hiatus between December and May so I could actually prepare for the. IIT exam. I hadn't even thought about it. So, those five months I prepared and then. You know, it just happened that I got it. When did you decide to do electronics? So that you know, the IIT system you had to pick the branch and so when you are suddenly. Asked to pick the branch, again it was just based on very naive notions. So, I felt that. You know, being small and you know, not very maybe strong, I should not do mechanical engineering. I was not aware enough at the time. But once I joined the electronics team here in those five years, of course, I became fully. Aware. Radhakshan Rao, Professor Venkat Rao. These were the people who really you know... Very big names even today. Still in my mind fresh in their classes and so on. To drop the idea but these people said fine let me go into communication so I wrote to. Everybody that I'll I also went to the library looked up communications looked okay to me. It's mathematics and all that looked like I could follow yeah so I realized yeah but. I but I figured that I could deal with it maths was not some was a fairly strong subject. So physics and maths so I said I could so I wrote that when I went there actually I. Did not do my PhD in wireless because the university I went to the faculty member who. Who I hired as my advisor, he was working in another new area which is what led to what. Today you have as MP, this JPEG, JPG and MP4 and all that, the video, with compression. So I worked in that because that was also a new area and something I didn't know and. That was what he was doing. And it was very practical. It was very practical and I worked in that and I did my PhD in that. But he had just come from Bell Labs, he had just joined academia when I went actually. And he had worked on a multitude of things. He had worked on wireless, he had worked on modems. So when I was discussing with him about what I should do after my PhD, I told him that. I am going back. I need a little bit of experience before I go back because I want to pick up whatever. I can. So I said, you know... But you wanted to be an academic. Yeah. Why did you choose going to Bell Labs? I said I want to learn a few more things. This is one thing I have done in my PhD. I don't want to go back just with this. I want to learn something else, some other field. So he was very helpful in that. He understood what I wanted to do and then he actually contacted his former colleagues. In Bell Labs and in the wireless area and told them this guy wants to learn wireless. He's done his PhD in this. Actually the people in Bell Labs in the video compression area were also asking me to join. As a full-time employee and because I knew the stuff but I told them I don't want to. Do this. You refused. Because I want to learn something else. I'm going back and need to arm myself. So I said wireless I don't know much because even in that University in the. US I had one course but that's about it. So I he sent me to this former. Colleague of his who I who interviewed me and I told him bluntly look I want to. Learn this stuff I have not done research in this I want to learn this. Stuff this is all I know about it and I'm willing to take a hit you know you. Don't give me a if it doesn't matter if you don't take me as a full-time. Employee give me a postdoctoral position is fine. So he gave me a postdoctoral. Position and I joined his group and there were all these stalwarts in wireless. Nobody very easily says to know to Bell laboratory. You had that that... I was very clear I wanted to come back. In fact, I never applied for a green card. It was just because that you were clear that you wanted to come back. I had decided. I had decided. I never had a second thought. I had decided. In fact, my advisor even asked me once more before I left the university. Left the university, are you sure? I said, because he'd seen so many Indians, he had friends. I said, I am very clear. So then, all the people who mentored me in Bell Labs,. Because in Bell Labs, what happened is,. When I went there, they realized what I was up to,. And so, actually, they were very kind. There were three wireless stalwarts in our group. Each one of them mentored me for six months. I worked with each one of them for six months. On a different problem, in a different area,. Learned each one of those things. Literally, like a guru, sishya thing. Because they knew this is what I wanted. So, six months with, you know... And you knew what they want from you? Well, they just wanted me to work with them and produce some good work. You know, produce a good paper. And we produced one paper each and that was it. You produced three papers? Yeah, in 18 months. In 18 months. And then you come back to India and immediately inducted in IIT Delhi? Yeah, I started right corresponding with the people here and so I... it turned out in those days they were not recruiting as regularly as they do now. They do now. So, at the time I wanted to come back, they had not advertised. So, I came as a visiting faculty member, took a little bit of a chance. Came as a visiting faculty member. Within a year, the advertisement came, I applied. Fortunately, I got selected and then I joined the faculty. We'll come back to that. Don't go anywhere. It's a short break. We'll come back. Welcome back. Dr. Bhaskar, when you came back to India, you joined as assistant professor and then climbed the ladder as it is called. And you became dean in your institution where you had studied. So half of your life you have probably spent in IIT Delhi. IIT Madras actually. IIT Madras and now you are director of the institute. You had a vision that India needs IITs and the IITs should do fundamental basic research. On the one end and then also do things which are required to change the conditions of the. Common man. How much have you been able to translate into practice? So one of the things that sort of ambitions that I had after I joined the faculty. Let me just add, IITs even today are seen as ivory towers, as isolated places, tapu. Where you can't even touch or go in. So how are you trying to translate? So I think one of the things that I had said, you know, one of the goals I had sort of as. What would be really ambitions to achieve was after I joined here was not just to teach. Well, publish some papers and guide some students but actually build some things, make some. Things because I knew that in India in electronics we were not making much, you know and to tell. You honestly even in you know in the US it's you're such a part of such a big cog in such. A big wheel you know big machine that you really don't even if you do a PhD even I was. In Bell Labs and I really learned how to build anything that division was somewhere else. You know, where they actually built the wireless systems. So I wanted to learn how to do that and I felt I could manage on my own now without. Any formal guidance. So we actually, I started taking on projects and so on and so then I learned that you could. Actually work with the team and build products and do things that could be relevant to the. Country to the industry here or to the people here and so on. And that initially of course I was confined to what I was learning and what I knew which. Is wireless communications and telecom and so some of us formed a group called the Telecom. And Networking Group, Professor Jhunjhunwala, myself, Professor Gonzales and we started. Building products with students you know. We started, the students started forming companies, that time we didn't know the word incubation. And we started trying to get take to the market and so on. You know try to get stuff and our wireless local loop product was quite successful actually,. BSNL deployed it in a big way, it was spread in many other countries. So we learnt, we actually got the confidence that we could actually build things that people. Would actually buy. We also understood how big the gaps are in the country when it comes to electronics,. Which are the buses we have missed and all of that we understood. So we started participating more and more in Delhi with ministries and so on. Once I became dean and director, I realised that this kind of a situation... Because before that, one of your papers became the basis for what is known as Wi-Fi today. And is seen everywhere. No, that's not quite correct. The early papers in Bell Labs, you are right, the early work in Bell Labs finally led to. Wi-Fi. But once I came back here, I left that stream of work. Were you excited? Yes, sure. When Wi-Fi came, I realized that it's coming from these things that we did in 1985. So in India whatever expertise you had gained in United States of America, you started applying. Here for making products. One of the products would you like to talk about? Yeah, so we made this thing called the Kodak wireless local loop. And you know it came from a line of thinking which now we apply it in all disciplines in. You know and especially as director I am working with so many of my colleagues to do this which. Is what does it you know if you have some if you like you take what was it at that time. We said why does India have only 8 million telephone lines? Why don't we have, why doesn't everybody have a telephone line? Even China has now at that time started expanding the telephone network in a big way. And the answer was very clear. At that time it cost 30,000 rupees to lay a telephone wire into the ground for each. Individual. And at that investment, the kind of revenue you need to generate, most people couldn't. Afford to pay those kind of bills. So people never had telephones. Then we said well what else can you do? It does cost that much to lay cables on the ground. So then we said, OK, why not we use wireless to connect people, give telephones to people,. Not cell phones, because that had not yet come. It had come in the West, not yet come to India. It was very expensive. And so we said, why not use the same technology but build fixed telephone lines, except you. Don't have to lay wires. And we found that if you do it right, you could do it at a third of the price. You could do it at 10,000 rupees a line. And at 10,000 rupees, the amount of money, billing you have to generate per month was. Such that a lot more, 100 million people in India would afford telephones, not 900 million. As with cell phones today. That is what you estimated at that time. So we actually coined a slogan that we want to make India have 100 million lines and we. Started building this wireless local loop as it's called. No other major Western country needed it because they already had telephones. So we built that and we deployed it in BSNL, BSNL deployed about half a million lines,. It was deployed abroad but just... And that brought communication revolution in India. Started with it. But you know, then what happened is the cellular revolution came and we were not part of that. Because we were not in India equipped to make the miniature phones at that time. In fact, we actually, in our group, we did make one phone just to learn how to do it. But it's not something, looking back, it's not something you can do in an academic environment. And we did it. We actually have it in my room. It works. But you know, we were, that bus we were missing. And finally, it came from abroad, of course. Cellular revolution brought prices down even further by a factor from 10,000 to a couple. Of thousand and that's why 900 million people in India have phones now. But what we did at that time started the wireless telephone revolution. Some people today would argue that a lot of independence was given to IITs and that's. Why and a lot of money was given to IITs that's why they could do much better than other institutions. And there is evidence for that. Do you think that the money flow as well as the independence is under threat? No, I don't think the independence is under threat. I think the IITs from the time they were conceived were always given academic independence. Nobody tells the IITs what to teach, how to teach it, when to change the curriculum and. So on and so forth, how to pick the students, what to do. And that is still true. I don't think that is under threat at all. The way we select our faculty, we just select the best that are available and when a faculty. Member teaches a course here, even as director, I do not have the authority to tell him or. Her what to teach, how to teach, whom to pass, whom to fail. It's their own decision and we don't interfere. So that academic freedom which percolates down to the classroom is not under threat. At all. Financially, I think, you know, the IITs looking back have been given generous funds whenever. Funds are available at the government when the things are tight sure you feel the pulling. Back there's no doubt about it there was a huge cut back in the 90 early 90s when India. Had the crisis 90 before 91 when when there was when there were good times in the 2000. 2005 period we were given a lot of money 2008 and so on now there's again we are feeling. A slight pulling back but I think this is we have to go with the country everybody feels. That do you think that other institutions are coming up and they are demanding their. And because of that... No, no. I think India is a big country and we need lots of institutions of all kinds. And my feeling is they all need support and the pie has to grow. I mean, really,. India can... Indians cannot get out of their poverty unless the pie grows. And question is, of course, how fast is it growing? That's why people keep talking about growth rates. And when it grows fast, you can do things faster. When it grows slower, you have to trim your sales. There's no doubt about it. And you also have to enlarge the base. Base. In fact, five IITs couldn't do so. Yeah, sure. This is a big country. It's like Europe, you know. Every European country has a couple of IITs, equivalent. So, your contribution personally has been. Recognized by the country, has been recognized by peers, scientists, students. Which one of. The recognition that you got, you value most? Well, all the awards mean a lot, especially the first award that I got, I think recognition. That I got from somebody outside the institute. The most valued ones are from your teachers. When a teacher calls you and says, I think you should become an academic and you should. Actually come back to this institute, you know, it was like, okay, that's great. That's an honour, ultimate honour. Ultimate honour. But beyond that, from outsiders, people who don't know you from Adam, the first award. Was VASVIK award and I was quite surprised because I had never realized somebody actually. Watching what I was doing. But finally this year recently I got, I was elevated the fellowship of the IEEE. IEEE is a very, very you know cherished organization in the world, it's almost so single organization. That of that size and of the peer group of electrical engineers and they don't award. Their fellowships easily and what was most satisfying was, the fellows, the citation. Is for the says it's for wireless developing wireless technology in India and that means. A lot to me because that's really what I set out to do when I came back and I had no idea. I could do how to do it because I had till that day I had not built anything and so it. Learned how to do it here so at extent it actually recognizes what I set out to do I'm. But I also recognize that compared to somebody who built wireless technology of the latest. Variety in the US or. You know the last 10 years or in Europe. This is a different thing but. In the context in which I did. It and the context in which I wanted to do it so. Badly it was the fact that that. Has been recognized is very satisfying to me. This is for the second time. That I am listening this argument. That most. Satisfactory thing is that. You are being watched somebody. Knows your work and. Knows its worth. It's been wonderful. Would you like to sign off by giving a message to younger generation? I think the message that I'd like to give to the younger generation is that. Not worry about what we are getting for ourselves but try to do something for others. You know, try to do, just in my case I was really focused on what can I do when I come back here,. What can I do in India, what can I do to do something here that has not been done before,. What can I do that will be actually not just that's not been done before that can actually benefit. In some way, I mean, I'm not an expert at it. But in some way if it leaves a positive contribution that will give me satisfaction. Once you have that kind of a focus then it usually happens and. It could be any other kind of focus in the current generation might want to be an entrepreneur might want to have a store. I want to create a company and you know generate employment for thousands, whatever it is. I think to have that kind of a focus on others rather than on oneself. This is the last part of the message. I think this combination always wins. Have a focus in life. Work for others. That will be the ultimate. Satisfaction in life. Thank you very much. Thank you, sir. May I on your behalf promise our viewers that you will be. Ready to answer any question that they have? Absolutely. If you have any question,. Comment or query, please do write to us at. Eureka rstv gmail.com we'll come back next week once again.
